query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and accumulation. The severe lattice distortion and local short-range order in these multilayers hinder dislocation glide within the bulk of the layers, forcing dislocations to be generated at and pile up along the layer interfaces. This dislocation accumulation gradually weakens the interfaces, enabling enhanced creep (progressive plastic deformation) compared to a state where these barriers are less severe.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers in the as-deposited or as-processed condition, characterized by significant lattice distortions and pronounced short-range order.
generation.intervention: A controlled modification of the interfacial microstructure achieved by a post-deposition annealing treatment (or a compositional tweak in one of the layers) designed to reduce the short-range order and lattice distortion at the interfaces without altering the overall multilayer architecture.
generation.conditions: Creep testing under constant sustained stress at an elevated temperature (e.g., a temperature high enough to activate dislocation motion but below that causing full microstructural recovery, such as 0.4–0.6 Tm) in an inert atmosphere to isolate the mechanical effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between the FCC and BCC layers, where dislocation nucleation and subsequent pile-ups occur as a result of hindered glide within the disordered layer interiors.
generation.mechanism: Because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and local short-range order impede the conventional dislocation glide within individual layers, the multilayer architecture directs dislocations to the interfaces. Under sustained loading, these dislocations nucleate and gradually accumulate at the interfaces, which eventually leads to interface weakening and progressive plastic deformation (creep). The annealing or compositional intervention is expected to reduce the short-range order at these interfaces, mitigating dislocation pile-up.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline multilayer, the treated sample with reduced short-range order/lattice distortion at the interfaces should exhibit a lower creep rate and less pronounced progressive plastic deformation over an equivalent testing period.
generation.baseline: Untreated FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coating with high lattice distortion and pronounced short-range order at the interfaces, subjected to constant sustained stress at elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where creep deformation is dominated by dislocation processes (i.e., temperatures high enough for dislocation movement but not so high as to cause diffusion-dominated or recovery processes) and where the nanoscale multilayer structure is preserved.
generation.uncertainty: The relative importance of short-range order versus lattice distortion as the primary factor impeding dislocation glide remains uncertain, as does the quantitative effect of the interfacial modification on creep behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers: one as the baseline with the as-deposited high short-range order and lattice distortion and one with a designed post-deposition annealing (or compositional adjustment) aimed at reducing short-range order at the interfaces. Subject both sets to creep tests under identical conditions (constant stress, elevated temperature, inert atmosphere). Use high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to monitor dislocation density and interface structural integrity over time.
measurements: Dislocation density and distribution at layer interfaces (via TEM)
Quantification of short-range order and lattice distortion at interfaces (via atom probe or high-resolution STEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention sample (with reduced SRO/lattice distortion) exhibits a creep rate and interfacial dislocation behavior statistically indistinguishable from the baseline, then the hypothesis that interfacial dislocation pile-up controlled by severe lattice distortion and SRO governs progressive plastic deformation would be falsified.
